# Introduction

Amazon knows very little about a customer beyond what's collected at
sign-up: name, email, phone, age, address. It has no idea how many people
actually live in that household or share the account. That's a problem,
because household size is useful for a lot of things - predicting spending
power, figuring out what kinds of products to recommend, etc. This project
uses the survey data as a stand-in for a third-party data provider: the
survey links a household-size answer to a person's full Amazon order
history, and the goal is to train a model on that link so it can predict
household size for the 2,000 respondents whose label was withheld for the
Kaggle leaderboard. The tricky part is that the test set only gives us
`Q.demos.gender` and `Q.demos.state` - none of the other survey questions
are available - so basically all of the useful signal has to come out of
`amazon-purchases.csv` itself: how often someone orders, how much they
spend, and what kind of things they buy (toys, baby items, pet food, etc.)
all seemed like reasonable proxies for how many people are in the house.
Submissions are scored with RMSE, as defined on the competition page.

# Setup: Libraries and Random Seed

```{r libraries}
set.seed(101)

library(data.table)   # the purchase log has ~1.85M rows, need something fast
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(glmnet)        # ridge / lasso
library(randomForest)  # random forest + variable importance
library(gbm)           # gradient boosting, ended up being the final model
```

# Data Loading

```{r load-data}
survey <- fread("survey_train_test.csv")
amz    <- fread("amazon-purchases.csv")

dim(survey)
dim(amz)
```

`survey` has one row per respondent. `test == TRUE` marks the 2,000
respondents that make up the Kaggle test set (their survey answers besides
gender/state are blank), and `test == FALSE` marks the 3,027 respondents
that have a labeled `Q.amazon.use.hh.size.num`. `amz` is the raw order
history - one row per item purchased - for all 5,027 respondents, linked
by `Survey ResponseID`.

# Feature Engineering

Since the test set doesn't give us much demographic info to work with, most
of the effort here goes into building behavioral features out of the
purchase log: how much someone orders and spends, how spread out their
orders are over time, how many different categories they buy from, and
what share of their orders fall into categories that seemed like they'd
correlate with household size (toys, baby products, pet food, etc.).

```{r feature-engineering}
amz[, spend := `Purchase Price Per Unit` * Quantity]
amz[, Category := ifelse(Category == "" | is.na(Category), "UNKNOWN", Category)]
amz[, `Order Date` := as.Date(`Order Date`)]

# use the 150 most common categories for the category-share features below
top_cats <- amz[, .N, by = Category][order(-N)][1:150, Category]

# one row per respondent, summarizing their order/spend/quantity behavior
base_agg <- amz[, .(
  n_orders        = .N,
  total_spend     = sum(spend, na.rm = TRUE),
  avg_price       = mean(`Purchase Price Per Unit`, na.rm = TRUE),
  median_price    = median(`Purchase Price Per Unit`, na.rm = TRUE),
  max_price       = max(`Purchase Price Per Unit`, na.rm = TRUE),
  std_price       = sd(`Purchase Price Per Unit`, na.rm = TRUE),
  total_qty       = sum(Quantity, na.rm = TRUE),
  avg_qty         = mean(Quantity, na.rm = TRUE),
  n_distinct_cat  = uniqueN(Category),
  first_order     = min(`Order Date`, na.rm = TRUE),
  last_order      = max(`Order Date`, na.rm = TRUE),
  n_states        = uniqueN(`Shipping Address State`)
), by = `Survey ResponseID`]

setnames(base_agg, "Survey ResponseID", "Survey.ResponseID")
base_agg[is.na(std_price), std_price := 0]   # happens when someone has exactly 1 order

max_date <- max(amz$`Order Date`, na.rm = TRUE)
base_agg[, span_days        := as.numeric(pmax(last_order - first_order, 1))]
base_agg[, orders_per_month := n_orders / (span_days / 30 + 1)]
base_agg[, spend_per_order  := total_spend / n_orders]
base_agg[, qty_per_order    := total_qty / n_orders]
base_agg[, cat_diversity    := n_distinct_cat / n_orders]
base_agg[, recency_days     := as.numeric(max_date - last_order)]
base_agg[, tenure_days      := as.numeric(max_date - first_order)]
base_agg[, spend_per_day    := total_spend / pmax(tenure_days, 1)]
base_agg[, orders_per_day   := n_orders / pmax(tenure_days, 1)]
base_agg[, log_total_spend  := log1p(total_spend)]
base_agg[, log_n_orders     := log1p(n_orders)]
base_agg[, log_total_qty    := log1p(total_qty)]
base_agg[, first_order := NULL]
base_agg[, last_order  := NULL]

# a few keyword-based category groups I picked out by hand, since these
# seemed like the clearest household-composition proxies in the data
baby_cats <- grep("BABY|INFANT|TODDLER", unique(amz$Category), value = TRUE)
pet_cats  <- grep("PET",                 unique(amz$Category), value = TRUE)
toy_cats  <- grep("TOY",                 unique(amz$Category), value = TRUE)
kid_cats  <- grep("CHILDREN",            unique(amz$Category), value = TRUE)

group_stats <- function(cats, prefix) {
  sub <- amz[Category %in% cats]
  g <- sub[, .(orders = .N, qty = sum(Quantity, na.rm = TRUE)), by = `Survey ResponseID`]
  setnames(g, c("Survey.ResponseID", paste0(prefix, "_orders"), paste0(prefix, "_qty")))
  g
}
baby_g <- group_stats(baby_cats, "baby")
pet_g  <- group_stats(pet_cats,  "pet")
toy_g  <- group_stats(toy_cats,  "toy")
kid_g  <- group_stats(kid_cats,  "kidcostume")

# for each respondent, what fraction of their orders fall in each top category
amz_top <- amz[Category %in% top_cats]
cat_counts <- dcast(amz_top, `Survey ResponseID` ~ Category,
                     fun.aggregate = length, value.var = "Category")
setnames(cat_counts, "Survey ResponseID", "Survey.ResponseID")
cnt_cols <- setdiff(names(cat_counts), "Survey.ResponseID")
row_totals <- rowSums(cat_counts[, ..cnt_cols])
cat_props <- copy(cat_counts)
for (cl in cnt_cols) cat_props[[cl]] <- cat_counts[[cl]] / row_totals
setnames(cat_props, cnt_cols, paste0("prop_", cnt_cols))

# glue it all together into one feature table, one row per respondent
purchase_feats <- merge(base_agg, cat_props, by = "Survey.ResponseID", all.x = TRUE, sort = FALSE)
purchase_feats <- merge(purchase_feats, baby_g, by = "Survey.ResponseID", all.x = TRUE, sort = FALSE)
purchase_feats <- merge(purchase_feats, pet_g,  by = "Survey.ResponseID", all.x = TRUE, sort = FALSE)
purchase_feats <- merge(purchase_feats, toy_g,  by = "Survey.ResponseID", all.x = TRUE, sort = FALSE)
purchase_feats <- merge(purchase_feats, kid_g,  by = "Survey.ResponseID", all.x = TRUE, sort = FALSE)

dim(purchase_feats)
```

Now I merge these onto the survey table. A handful of respondents (about 10
out of 5,027) never made a single Amazon purchase, so they end up with `NA`
for every purchase feature - I fill those with 0, since "zero orders in
this category" is a real, meaningful value rather than something missing.

```{r merge-and-fill}
df <- merge(survey, purchase_feats, by = "Survey.ResponseID", all.x = TRUE, sort = FALSE)

num_cols <- setdiff(names(purchase_feats), "Survey.ResponseID")
for (c in num_cols) set(df, which(is.na(df[[c]])), c, 0)

# gender is available for every respondent, so it's cheap to include
# (state gets dropped later - see Preprocessing for why)
df[, gender_male   := as.integer(Q.demos.gender == "Male")]
df[, gender_female := as.integer(Q.demos.gender == "Female")]

table(df$test)
```

# Exploratory Data Analysis

```{r eda-target-dist, fig.cap="Distribution of the household-size response variable in the training set."}
train_only <- df[test == FALSE]

ggplot(train_only, aes(x = factor(Q.amazon.use.hh.size.num))) +
  geom_bar(fill = "#4C72B0") +
  labs(title = "Distribution of Household Size (Training Set)",
       x = "Household size (4 = 4 or more)", y = "Number of respondents") +
  theme_minimal()
```

The response is capped at 4 since the survey question tops out at "4+", so
it's really a four-level ordinal variable rather than an open-ended count.
Two-person households are the most common, with single-person and
four-or-more households both fairly common too. I used this to justify
clipping every model's predictions to `[1, 4]` later on, since going
outside that range can only hurt the RMSE.

```{r eda-orders, fig.cap="Number of Amazon orders by household size."}
ggplot(train_only, aes(x = factor(Q.amazon.use.hh.size.num), y = n_orders)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "#DD8452") +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, quantile(train_only$n_orders, 0.95))) +
  labs(title = "Number of Amazon Orders vs. Household Size",
       x = "Household size", y = "Total number of orders") +
  theme_minimal()
```

Bigger households order slightly more on average, but the boxes overlap a
lot across all four groups. Order count by itself is a pretty weak signal -
I noticed this early on and it's a big part of why I ended up building
dozens of more specific features instead of leaning on a couple of obvious
ones like total orders or total spend.

```{r eda-spend, fig.cap="Log total spend by household size."}
ggplot(train_only, aes(x = factor(Q.amazon.use.hh.size.num), y = log1p(total_spend))) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "#55A868") +
  labs(title = "Log Total Spend vs. Household Size",
       x = "Household size", y = "log(1 + total spend)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

Total spend (log-scaled here since it's heavily skewed) tells basically the
same story as order count, which isn't surprising given how correlated the
two are with each other. Neither one does a great job separating the four
groups on its own.

```{r eda-toys, fig.cap="Share of orders in the toys-and-games category by household size."}
ggplot(train_only, aes(x = factor(Q.amazon.use.hh.size.num), y = prop_TOYS_AND_GAMES)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "#C44E52") +
  labs(title = "Share of Orders in TOYS_AND_GAMES vs. Household Size",
       x = "Household size", y = "Proportion of orders") +
  theme_minimal()
```

This one's more interesting - the share of a respondent's orders that go
toward toys and games climbs pretty steadily with household size, and it
turned out to be the single most correlated numeric feature I found. Makes
sense intuitively: bigger households are more likely to have kids in them,
and toy purchases are a decent stand-in for that.

```{r eda-baby, fig.cap="Household size composition by presence of baby-category purchases."}
train_only[, has_baby_purchase := ifelse(is.na(baby_orders) | baby_orders == 0, "No", "Yes")]

ggplot(train_only, aes(x = has_baby_purchase, fill = factor(Q.amazon.use.hh.size.num))) +
  geom_bar(position = "fill") +
  labs(title = "Household Size Composition by Presence of Baby-Category Purchases",
       x = "Ever purchased a baby-related product", y = "Proportion of respondents",
       fill = "Household size") +
  theme_minimal()
```

Respondents who've ever bought something baby-related (car seats, formula,
bottles, and so on) skew noticeably toward the 3-4 person households
compared to everyone else. This is the kind of narrow, life-stage-specific
signal that a broad feature like order count just can't pick up.

```{r eda-pet, fig.cap="Share of orders in the pet-food category by household size."}
ggplot(train_only, aes(x = factor(Q.amazon.use.hh.size.num), y = prop_PET_FOOD)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "#8172B2") +
  labs(title = "Share of Orders in PET_FOOD vs. Household Size",
       x = "Household size", y = "Proportion of orders") +
  theme_minimal()
```

Pet food share goes up a little with household size too, though it's a
noisier relationship than toys or baby products. That tracks - having a pet
correlates with having a bigger household, but plenty of small households
have pets too, so I expected this feature to matter less in the final
model.

```{r eda-gender, fig.cap="Household size composition by gender."}
ggplot(train_only, aes(x = Q.demos.gender, fill = factor(Q.amazon.use.hh.size.num))) +
  geom_bar(position = "fill") +
  labs(title = "Household Size Composition by Gender",
       x = "Gender", y = "Proportion of respondents", fill = "Household size") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1))
```

Gender is available for every single respondent, including the whole test
set, but on its own it barely moves the household-size distribution. I kept
it in anyway since it's free (no missing values to worry about), just not
expecting it to do much heavy lifting.

```{r eda-corr, fig.cap="Correlation of selected engineered features with household size.", fig.height=5}
numeric_candidates <- c("n_orders", "total_spend", "total_qty", "n_distinct_cat",
                         "orders_per_month", "span_days", "tenure_days",
                         "prop_TOYS_AND_GAMES", "prop_TOY_FIGURE", "prop_PET_FOOD",
                         "prop_HEADPHONES", "cat_diversity")

corr_vals <- sapply(numeric_candidates, function(v) {
  cor(train_only[[v]], train_only$Q.amazon.use.hh.size.num, use = "complete.obs")
})
corr_df <- data.frame(feature = names(corr_vals), correlation = as.numeric(corr_vals))
corr_df <- corr_df[order(-abs(corr_df$correlation)), ]

ggplot(corr_df, aes(x = reorder(feature, abs(correlation)), y = correlation)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#4C72B0") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(title = "Correlation of Selected Engineered Features with Household Size",
       x = NULL, y = "Correlation with Q.amazon.use.hh.size.num") +
  theme_minimal()
```

This lines up with the boxplots above - toy and family-category shares beat
out the general activity features (`n_orders`, `total_spend`) in raw
correlation. That said, every single correlation here is under 0.2 in
absolute value, so I went into modeling knowing this was going to be a
noisy, hard-to-predict target, which is really the whole reason I leaned
toward flexible non-linear models instead of trusting a plain linear fit.

# Preprocessing

There are three preprocessing choices worth explaining here:

1. **Missing purchase history.** As mentioned above, respondents with zero
   Amazon purchases get 0 for every purchase feature instead of `NA` - see
   the `merge-and-fill` chunk. Treating "no purchases" as missing data
   didn't make sense to me since it's a real and informative outcome.
2. **Dropping `Q.demos.state`.** State is available for every respondent,
   so it's tempting to use it, but one-hot encoding it means adding about
   50 mostly-empty indicator columns. When I tried this in cross-validation
   it consistently made RMSE slightly worse - the extra columns seem to
   just add noise without any real predictive payoff, so I left it out and
   kept only gender as a demographic feature.
3. **Feature selection.** After all the engineering above I ended up with
   roughly 180 numeric features but only 3,027 labeled training rows, and
   none of them are strongly predictive on their own (see the correlation
   plot). That's a recipe for tree-based models overfitting to noise, so I
   fit a quick random forest on the full training set just to rank features
   by importance, then restricted every candidate model below to the top
   45. This cut cross-validated RMSE noticeably compared to using all ~180
   features.

```{r feature-selection}
meta_cols <- c("Survey.ResponseID", "Q.demos.age", "Q.demos.hispanic", "Q.demos.race",
  "Q.demos.education", "Q.demos.income", "Q.demos.gender", "Q.sexual.orientation",
  "Q.demos.state", "Q.amazon.use.howmany", "Q.amazon.use.hh.size",
  "Q.amazon.use.hh.size.num", "Q.amazon.use.how.oft", "Q.substance.use.cigarettes",
  "Q.substance.use.marijuana", "Q.substance.use.alcohol", "Q.personal.diabetes",
  "Q.personal.wheelchair", "Q.life.changes", "Q.sell.YOUR.data", "Q.sell.consumer.data",
  "Q.small.biz.use", "Q.census.use", "Q.research.society", "test")

feature_cols <- setdiff(names(df), meta_cols)
length(feature_cols)

train <- df[test == FALSE]
test_df  <- df[test == TRUE]

X <- as.matrix(train[, ..feature_cols])
y <- train$Q.amazon.use.hh.size.num

set.seed(101)
rf_screen <- randomForest(x = X, y = y, ntree = 300,
                           mtry = floor(sqrt(ncol(X))), nodesize = 15)
importance_ranked <- sort(importance(rf_screen)[, 1], decreasing = TRUE)
top_feats <- names(importance_ranked)[1:45]

X_sel      <- X[, top_feats]
X_test_sel <- as.matrix(test_df[, ..top_feats])

head(importance_ranked, 15)
```

# Candidate Models

I tried five candidate models, all using the same 45 selected features,
evaluated with 5-fold cross-validation on the training set. RMSE is
computed on each held-out fold and predictions are clipped to `[1, 4]`
before scoring, since the response never falls outside that range anyway.

| Model identifier | Type                      | Variables        | Hyperparameters |
|-------------------|---------------------------|-------------------|------------------|
| M1_ridge          | Ridge regression (glmnet) | top 45 features   | alpha = 0, lambda chosen by internal CV |
| M2_lasso          | Lasso regression (glmnet) | top 45 features   | alpha = 1, lambda chosen by internal CV |
| M3_rf             | Random forest             | top 45 features   | ntree = 500, mtry = p/3, nodesize = 10 |
| M4_gbm_shallow    | Gradient boosted trees    | top 45 features   | n.trees = 250, depth = 2, shrinkage = 0.02 |
| M5_gbm_tuned      | Gradient boosted trees    | top 45 features   | n.trees = 300, depth = 3, shrinkage = 0.02, bag.fraction = 0.6 |

```{r cv-setup}
rmse <- function(pred, actual) sqrt(mean((pred - actual)^2))

set.seed(42)
k <- 5
folds <- sample(rep(1:k, length.out = nrow(X_sel)))
```

```{r cv-ridge}
ridge_scores <- c()
for (i in 1:k) {
  tr <- which(folds != i); va <- which(folds == i)
  m <- cv.glmnet(X_sel[tr, ], y[tr], alpha = 0)
  p <- pmin(pmax(as.numeric(predict(m, X_sel[va, ], s = "lambda.min")), 1), 4)
  ridge_scores <- c(ridge_scores, rmse(p, y[va]))
}
```

```{r cv-lasso}
lasso_scores <- c()
for (i in 1:k) {
  tr <- which(folds != i); va <- which(folds == i)
  m <- cv.glmnet(X_sel[tr, ], y[tr], alpha = 1)
  p <- pmin(pmax(as.numeric(predict(m, X_sel[va, ], s = "lambda.min")), 1), 4)
  lasso_scores <- c(lasso_scores, rmse(p, y[va]))
}
```

```{r cv-rf}
rf_scores <- c()
for (i in 1:k) {
  tr <- which(folds != i); va <- which(folds == i)
  m <- randomForest(x = X_sel[tr, ], y = y[tr], ntree = 500,
                     mtry = floor(ncol(X_sel) / 3), nodesize = 10)
  p <- pmin(pmax(predict(m, X_sel[va, ]), 1), 4)
  rf_scores <- c(rf_scores, rmse(p, y[va]))
}
```

```{r cv-gbm-shallow}
gbm_shallow_scores <- c()
for (i in 1:k) {
  tr <- which(folds != i); va <- which(folds == i)
  m <- gbm.fit(x = as.data.frame(X_sel[tr, ]), y = y[tr], distribution = "gaussian",
               n.trees = 250, interaction.depth = 2, shrinkage = 0.02,
               bag.fraction = 0.7, verbose = FALSE)
  p <- pmin(pmax(predict(m, as.data.frame(X_sel[va, ]), n.trees = 250), 1), 4)
  gbm_shallow_scores <- c(gbm_shallow_scores, rmse(p, y[va]))
}
```

```{r cv-gbm-tuned}
gbm_tuned_scores <- c()
for (i in 1:k) {
  tr <- which(folds != i); va <- which(folds == i)
  m <- gbm.fit(x = as.data.frame(X_sel[tr, ]), y = y[tr], distribution = "gaussian",
               n.trees = 300, interaction.depth = 3, shrinkage = 0.02,
               bag.fraction = 0.6, verbose = FALSE)
  p <- pmin(pmax(predict(m, as.data.frame(X_sel[va, ]), n.trees = 300), 1), 4)
  gbm_tuned_scores <- c(gbm_tuned_scores, rmse(p, y[va]))
}
```

# Model Evaluation and Tuning

```{r cv-results-table}
results_tbl <- data.frame(
  Model_identifier = c("M1_ridge", "M2_lasso", "M3_rf", "M4_gbm_shallow", "M5_gbm_tuned"),
  Mean_CV_RMSE = c(mean(ridge_scores), mean(lasso_scores), mean(rf_scores),
                    mean(gbm_shallow_scores), mean(gbm_tuned_scores))
)
results_tbl <- results_tbl[order(results_tbl$Mean_CV_RMSE), ]
knitr::kable(results_tbl, digits = 4, caption = "5-fold CV RMSE by candidate model")
```

```{r cv-results-plot, fig.cap="Cross-validated RMSE comparison across candidate models."}
ggplot(results_tbl, aes(x = reorder(Model_identifier, Mean_CV_RMSE), y = Mean_CV_RMSE)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#4C72B0") +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(min(results_tbl$Mean_CV_RMSE) * 0.97, max(results_tbl$Mean_CV_RMSE) * 1.01)) +
  labs(title = "Cross-Validated RMSE by Candidate Model",
       x = NULL, y = "Mean 5-fold CV RMSE") +
  coord_flip() +
  theme_minimal()
```

The two linear models (ridge, lasso) both trail the tree-based ones, which
tells me the relationship here isn't linear - something like "lots of
orders AND a high toy share" seems to matter more than either variable on
its own. `M5_gbm_tuned` comes out on top, with the shallow GBM and random
forest close behind. I went with the tuned GBM as my final model since the
gap held up consistently across folds rather than being driven by one or
two lucky splits.

# Final Model and Interpretation

I refit `M5_gbm_tuned` on the full training set (all 3,027 labeled
respondents, not just the CV folds) using the same hyperparameters found
above - more training data should only help, and there's no reason to
hold any of it back once the model is chosen.

```{r final-model}
set.seed(101)
final_model <- gbm.fit(x = as.data.frame(X_sel), y = y, distribution = "gaussian",
                        n.trees = 300, interaction.depth = 3, shrinkage = 0.02,
                        bag.fraction = 0.6, verbose = FALSE)
```

```{r final-importance, fig.cap="Top 15 feature importances for the final gradient boosting model.", fig.height=5}
imp_df <- summary(final_model, n.trees = 300, plotit = FALSE)
imp_df <- imp_df[1:15, ]

ggplot(imp_df, aes(x = reorder(var, rel.inf), y = rel.inf)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#DD8452") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(title = "Top 15 Feature Importances - Final GBM Model",
       x = NULL, y = "Relative influence (%)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

Toy- and baby-related purchase shares dominate the top of the importance
list, along with a few general engagement measures like `tenure_days`,
`span_days`, and `n_states`. That lines up with what I saw during EDA -
household-composition proxies carry more weight than raw order volume. My
guess for why tenure/span show up so high is that a longer purchase history
just gives the model a more reliable read on someone's typical behavior,
compared to a respondent with only a handful of orders on record.

```{r individual-predictions}
set.seed(7)
example_idx <- sample(1:nrow(train), 3)
example_feats <- c(imp_df$var[1:5])

examples <- train[example_idx, c("Survey.ResponseID", "Q.amazon.use.hh.size.num",
                                   example_feats), with = FALSE]
examples$predicted <- pmin(pmax(predict(final_model,
                          as.data.frame(X_sel[example_idx, ]), n.trees = 300), 1), 4)

knitr::kable(examples, digits = 2,
             caption = "Three example training respondents: top-5 feature values, actual, and predicted household size")
```

For these three respondents, the predictions move the way I'd expect given
their feature values - higher toy/family-category shares and longer
purchase tenure push the prediction toward a bigger household, while
respondents with little activity in those categories get pulled toward a
one- or two-person prediction. It's a small sample, but it's reassuring
that the model is behaving the way the importance ranking says it should,
rather than doing something I can't explain.

# Discussion of Final Model

**Model selection.** I went with `M5_gbm_tuned` - a gradient boosted tree
model on the top 45 features - because it had the lowest 5-fold CV RMSE of
the five candidates, and it beat the shallow GBM and random forest
consistently across folds rather than just on average.

**Strengths.** The model can pick up non-linear, interaction-heavy patterns
between purchase categories and household size that a linear model would
miss entirely, and it handles respondents with no purchase history
gracefully (their features are just 0, and the model has learned to treat
that as "low activity" rather than something broken).

**Weaknesses.** Honestly, the signal in this problem is just weak. Even the
best single feature I found correlates with household size at well under
0.2, so the model's CV RMSE of about 1.03 is only a modest improvement over
just predicting the training mean everywhere (which would land around
1.06-1.10, given the response's standard deviation of roughly 1.1).
Household size ultimately depends on things - family structure, life
stage, income - that purchase history can only partly stand in for.

**Possible improvements.** A few things that could plausibly help: ZIP-code
level shipping addresses (to bring in Census household-size statistics for
that area), order timestamps at the hour/day-of-week level (which might
expose shared-account usage patterns), and product-level metadata like
pack size or "family size" labeling that my category-share features only
partially capture.

# Generate Kaggle Submission

```{r generate-submission}
test_predictions <- pmin(pmax(predict(final_model, as.data.frame(X_test_sel), n.trees = 300), 1), 4)

submission <- data.frame(
  Survey.ResponseID = test_df$Survey.ResponseID,
  Q.amazon.use.hh.size.num = test_predictions
)

fwrite(submission, "submission.csv")
```
